Interviewer:	How are you any way?

Subject:	Not too bad just tired.

Interviewer:	OK hopefully it won’t take too long, can you tell me when you started on placement?

Subject:	Erm the middle of August, last year.

Interviewer:	So you’ve nearly finished now then?

Subject:	Yeah probably another month in May - 2 or 3 months something like that.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay can you tell me a bit about the company that you're working for?

Subject:	I’m working for [company], erm I can’t think at the moment. What, what sort of...?

Interviewer:	What, what do [company] do what?

Subject:	Erm there's it's got lots of different divisions, the bit that I'm working for is [Company] Civil Engineering. Erm I'm working at [name] Airport. They’ve got other jobs, they’ve got a couple of wind farms that they’re building at the moment. Mainly roads, I think they’re doing another airport as well.

Interviewer:	Ok, briefly how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Erm, the company itself I, I think you know encourages, I mean I have found sort of you know the higher management and stuff to be very encouraging towards, towards me. (Ok) Since I've been there.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay we’ll talk a bit about that a bit more about that in a minute. I've just got some questions now about how useful you think the course has been to the work that you're doing on placement and whether you think that there's any particular skills that have been useful?

Subject:	Erm, certain, I mean there's, some modules are more useful like the more practical modules. (Yeah) I've found them a lot more useful because I've gone out working for a contractor so I'm out on site so the practical stuff, it's more use. Erm, from what I've been told about the design and what I've learnt about the design, I think, some of the more of the theoretical would come into use there. So I think the course is generally, depending on what you go into, erm you know specific areas are more suitable.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay is there anything in particular that you wished you had learnt before you started placement?

Subject:	Erm, I because like I said I'm working out practically I wish I had actually had more experience in er using the instruments. Erm more practical because we had to use erm the first day I was there you know I just got sort of handed one and they were like ‘off you go’. And, it was a bit daunting but while I you know I could do it all but the first time you sort of do it it's a bit, ‘oh my gosh what am I doing’ you know? So I think a bit more practical experience in using instruments would have been helpful.

Interviewer:	OK were you taught anything about Health & Safety at university?

Subject:	Yeah we had well it's was again for those people going on their year out. We had erm, was it one or two sort of lectures. I think there's one big proper lecture and a little sort of reminder lecture about Health & Safety and erm you know what to look for and sort of your general Health & Safety and then a bit more site specific…

Interviewer:	OK, did you find that useful?

Subject:	Erm, fairly useful I mean most of it is just common sense really, all health and safety is just common sense. But it was, it was quite handy sort of to get a bit of a heads up before I walked on site instead of just being told of health and safety. So then when I did get sort of given the health & safety briefing on site I didn’t feel you know quite so new to site. And a lot of my questions had already sort of been answered.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah I think we should have had more site visits because the only site visits there were, were organised as part of the civil engineering society and I think the department and that you know going on that involved sort of missing lectures and stuff. And I think the department you know should organise it as compulsory you know some compulsory site visits? 

Interviewer:	Yeah so you just get the experience?

Subject:	Or not compulsory as such but you know you can go if you want to kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Yeah through the department rather than through the …

Subject:	Rather than having to miss lectures or anything.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay, how useful have you found, because I think you worked on site last summer, didn’t you?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	How useful has that been for being on placement now?

Subject:	Er, I think what I did last summer wasn’t really sort of related to being an engineer. I was working in a lab it wasn’t I mean it had helped that I had already done the sort of whole you know I was on site and I was used to being you know one of the only sort of females around. And I was coping with like working with lots of men and that, that kind of thing. Erm the actual work itself did help, has helped a little but it hasn’t made a sort of massive difference.	

Interviewer:	OK how did you find the transition from education to work was it easy or was it difficult like how was it starting doing nights and stuff?

Subject:	Erm, to begin with it was like all right and doing nights at first was quite exciting but then I just got to the stage where I was like ‘oh I need a holiday’, because I had been used to having you know sort of uni holidays? (Yeah) Sort of long breaks off and I did just get to the stage where I needed a holiday and now oh it's just a nightmare. I bet everyone is just sort of the same when you’ve just been on nights for so long and every week we’re like, ‘oh when are we finishing’? And then it's, ‘oh it will be a couple of weeks’ and we’ve been told that for like 2 months now so (cor blimey) it is sort of wearing on a bit now but erm adjusting to it wasn’t, wasn’t too bad. And like I still feel the same now, I mean part of the problems is because I'm working nights, I don't really get a proper weekend. (Yeah) So it's a bit, so it's not you know so I don't really get a sort of break at the weekends I only actually get one day when I'm not working. And I just sort of get to the stage like continuous work, I'm like, ‘oh I need a break, I need a holiday’.

Interviewer:	Yes okay, do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues at all like dealing with different types of people or office politics or anything like that?

Subject:	Yeah actually I have there was a erm they’d hired quite a few agency engineers I don't know if you know that. They're basically sort of freelance engineers that they just you know get hired in when the company is running short of engineers, they just get hired in. And there's a couple that I've worked with erm both of them sort of have had issues with working with me because I was a student. One of them more so than the other but he had issues with me because I was a student and I was a girl. (Right) And that was when I'm sort of struggling trying to learn that was actually very, I found that very difficult to deal with and I ended up having you know to go the manager and all sorts to get them to deal with it for me because I couldn’t do it myself.

Interviewer:	Ok that’s interesting, do you think that situation has helped you in the sense of thinking about how to deal with things like that in the future then?

Subject:	I think so because now it's made me realise that I mean because you know I was sort of you know like apologising for being a student and being a girl and now I'm just going to you know now I sort of say ‘well yes I am a student but everybody learns’. (Yeah) And I sort of feel that, that, that now is really my attitude and like yes I make mistakes and yes I don't know stuff but you know…

Interviewer:	You’ve got to start somewhere…

Subject:	And nobody was born knowing everything, everyone has got to learn.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay do you how, what would you say are the main ways that work and university differ?

Subject:	Erm, this makes me sound really lazy but things like you can't just sort of wake up in the morning and go, ‘oh I don't fancy going to work’. Like you can at the end of the day you can do that with your lectures you just go, ‘oh I'm not going in for that one’ and you don't go. (Yeah) So in that respect I think work you have a bigger commitment for work you know you have to go. You have to turn up like you have to be in at you have to be in like you know a fit state for work. You can't turn up like with a hangover or something. (Yeah) Erm you know you’ve got to be quite sort of I suppose keen and well presented rather than just sort of having a day when you just sort of stagger in and go through the motions or something and then go back to bed.

Interviewer:	Yeah do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals then?

Subject:	I think so yes er I think university is more about you know teaching and us learning whereas I think work at the end of the day is all more about getting the job done and spending as little money as possible doing it.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do [Company] employ many women?

Subject:	Erm, not they do I mean I think a couple of the sort of higher board members are women. They're having some sort of financial problems at the moment so there's like major re-shuffles going on. So, I can't though I know there was a couple but I can't specifically say whether they are still there. Not just because of the way it's being re-shuffled nothing sexist particularly. Erm I'm the only female [Company] employee, there's a couple of others who don't work directly for [Company] on site. (Right) Erm but when I have spoken to other people I mean the sort of sandwich students and the graduates that I met this year there was one other girl and I think there was 15 of us maybe. (Yeah) Maybe 20 people and there was one other girl there.

Interviewer:	Okay how have you found being one of the only women on site?

Subject:	Erm it doesn’t really bother me too much I mean you’ve got to you know you get the obvious sort of bits of well I’ve had bits of bother from people but once you know this is going to sound awfully racist and I don't mean it to be but a lot the sort of Asian, Indian there's an awful lot of Indian people and with their culture a lot of them aren’t used to having women around that tell them what to do. (Yeah) And I don't mean, that sounds terribly racist and I don't mean it to be. I do apologise but erm so I had a bit of a problem with a few of them at the start until they sort of realised that you know, until I sort of turned round and I was like, ‘I can tell you what to do and I am going to tell you what to do and when I tell you what to do you have to do what I say’. Because they have the support of other people you know if I sort of said , ‘well do this’ and they didn’t do it and then someone would come along to me and say, ‘why haven’t they done it’? And I would say, ‘well I did tell them’ then they sort of realised that I was all right. And you get the obvious you know bits of perving and stuff like that but you’ve just got to learn that take it in the spirit that it's meant. (Yeah) Because generally speaking people are having a laugh, trying to wind you up, trying to get a bit of a reaction from you and you’ve just got to sort of you know accept that’s all they're doing and you know sort of deal with it that way sort of you know go ‘yeah, yeah you're having a laugh’ and sort of laugh back at them.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay does the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students to follow? Like with any targets that you're supposed to achieve in the year that you're there?

Subject:	If they do I don't know, I haven’t heard of anything. I mean they, I have had sort of a form, I do remember having like a sort of little meeting and having like a form filled out you know a sort of 1 to 4, and how your ideas and coping and all that kind of generally how you cope with like stress and how you manage with erm, how you're managing with the work and how you're improving. I did have one like that but that was the limit to anything I've seen.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that it would be a good idea?

Subject:	I think so, I mean I have personally found my whole year out to be pretty disorganised and I don't know if this is the case with everybody and whether I'm you know, or whether everyone finds this, but I have personally found it to be very disorganised and like nobody has bothered to sort of do anything or think you know you’ve got stuff to do work to do for university, you bothered to say ‘oh right you need sort someone that’s like an external tutor’ and no one has sort of bothered to sort that out until I chased them up about it. (Yeah) So I would have preferred it you know if could have gone in and someone had been like right I'm your external tutor, do you have any university stuff you know sort of sort of you know, scooped me up on the first day as it were.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay have you been at the same site all year?

Subject:	No I was at another site again that was for 3 weeks. (OK) Again that was part of the kind of disorganised thing it wasn’t really suitable, in my eyes, for like an engineer it was more of a QS’s job because all the people there were QS’s and I and it was at the bottom of my road where I live at home quite literally. (Yes) So I felt that I got dumped there for a little while and then got you know I just felt like I just kind of got shunted around and then got dumped at Birmingham because there was a space.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay have you had any training at all while you’ve been on placement?

Subject:	Erm I've been on, I went on we got sent on a 2 week course away to the National Construction College. One week was a setting out and surveying week which is a sort of refresher course because that’s predominantly what we do on site and there's, the other week was it was called the Graduate Appreciation Course and that shows you a little bit of everything, like scaffolding and how to erect it and it's designed to make you not look like a complete idiot on site and so I found that really helpful. It was I mean one day of each type of thing isn’t much but the idea is that you can, you’ve got a vague idea what they’re talking about it.

Interviewer:	Yeah is that just people from [Company] or is that people from other companies as well on that?

Subject:	Erm, on ours other people can do it but on our particular course it was just [Company]. (Okay) But it's sort of a standard, standard course that gets done. (Yeah) Erm, I've been on a couple of courses ooh I forgotten what they're called, kind of like health and safety and policy systems and manual handling training courses. But they were more sort of generic, everybody in the company has to do this training course rather than sort of placement students or graduate specific training.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay what does your role within the company actually involve then?

Subject:	Erm, what I do or what I have been doing is erm on site we are responsible for the setting out which is the sort of placement of like I've been involved in the construction of the new (inaudible) at the airport. So, basically I had to set out the outline literally where it was going to be and we’re responsible for you know setting all that. Making sure that the levels for everything is correct, the positions of things is correct, it all you know happens at sort of the right time.

Interviewer:	Yeah is that the job that you expected to be doing when you got the placement then?

Subject:	I’ve actually had more responsibility than I was expecting but that is the kind of thing I was expecting to be doing yes.

Interviewer:	Ok do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility then?

Subject:	Erm yes and no, back in the beginning no, I felt I sort of got thrown in a bit at the deep end.

Interviewer:	Yeah like maybe you’d been given too much too soon?

Subject:	Yeah but what happened again I was working with an agency engineer and erm a lot of them you know they just like to sort of come in, get given say the information, set it out and leave. They don't like to chase it up or think about it, where it comes from, why. It's a bit difficult to explain but they just sort of want to go out on site and do the work there and not have you know they, like if any calculations need to be done, they just want to be sort of provided with a list of calculations and not doing them. (Yeah) So I sort of got, I started to get a bit stuck. (Yeah) Because I was trying to do then all of this work and I really didn’t know what I was doing, but and it's been like that for the whole time, but now because I had some problems a little while ago with all the agency engineers sort of not wanting to work for me because I’m a student. I'm now working with a [Company] engineer. (OK) Now I feel it's all right because I now have someone I can turn to and say ‘oh I'm not sure what I'm doing can you just come and help me’?

Interviewer:	Yeah okay erm how would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	Erm, in er I've enjoyed doing the actual work erm not too sure whether I want to go into civil engineering at the moment. (Right) But it, part of that may just be sort of you know because I'm still on nights. I mean it's kind of hard to describe quite how soul destroying it is doing that for 7 months. (Yes) Erm, it's been very stressful I think a lot of the time.

Interviewer:	Yeah and what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the placement then?

Subject:	Er the best thing is actually getting out and meeting the other people who are there doing engineering sort of my age and sort of going out and doing all right and cos’ I do sort of enjoy it. To me the worst bits have actually it's all sort of come down to the organisation of it. (Yeah) Because I just feel that if it had all been organised properly I’d have been sort of much happier and much more able just to relax and learn.

Interviewer:	Yes okay how would you say that the placement has met your expectations then?

Subject:	I think so yes I've got a very well I feel I've got a very sort of varied experience. Well I will have by the time I've finished in what I've been doing. Rather than just standing there doing the same things like just setting out this point and that point. I've you know I've been involved in sort of all different areas of the construction because I've been there right from the very start. I've been involved in all of the different things like the sort of black top laying and the drainage and constructing sort of electricity cable runs and things like that. So there's been lots of different areas I've been involved in sort of within one section as it were.

Interviewer:	Yes okay is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

Subject:	Erm, I'm not sure I mean I think I sort of came out, you know I sort expect that I’d know sort of a bit of a, to be able to just come out and do everything. (Yeah) Because when we sort of did you know surveying and setting out at uni I could just do it all, whereas coming out onto site when it's real and you don't always have the right information and bits are missing and it's sometimes it is just wrong. (Yeah) And there's things that I just that I still don't understand then I seem to think that’s the main thing. I just, it's not a bad thing it’ just I think that I sort of expected to just to do it all and I can't, but that’s quite a good thing that I’m learning it.

Interviewer:	OK what do you think are the main benefits of doing a placement are then?

Subject:	I think erm God like I said I'm not sure that I want to go into civil engineering erm I've got the rest of this year to think plus the next 2 years at university to think about it. (Yeah) And decide what I want to do so I think for people like me it helped because rather than having being in this situation when I've graduated, going ‘on no, what do I do now?’ I think it helps to sort it out and if you went into it and decided that you really loved it I think. Plus there's lots of the practical aspects that you can apply to all the theory now. Like the things I've learnt and well I can think about the work and think, ‘oh yeah well when he says that he actually means this because now I know what he’s talking about’. (Yeah) And hopefully when we go back and do more work I’ll be able to do it the other way around. (Yeah) And sort of theoretical I’ll then be able to think of the practical and think, ‘ah yeah well I remember doing this’. So you know and sort I will be able to sort of visualise the practical side.

Interviewer:	Yeah do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement then?

Subject:	Erm, I don't think so really I could only think it would be a drawback if you went into it and decided that you absolutely hated it but on the other hand again that would still be a good thing because you would have only sort of wasted a year as opposed to…

Interviewer:	Your whole career.

Subject:	Yeah. Erm no I don't think so.

Interviewer:	Ok do you think that you have changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	I think so I think I've grown up a bit, realised that things go wrong but even if I do it wrong it's not me personally even though I may have done it wrong it's not you know, if I get shouted at they're not, they're not shouting at me personally you know I get shouted at because I did it wrong but then that’s it, end of story. It doesn’t matter anymore that I did it wrong kind of thing you know you get told off, it doesn’t mater. You know get told you know, ‘concentrate next time’ and that’s it. (Yeah) So yeah I think I've grown up and learnt to or learning I should say not to take things quite so personally. Because in the beginning I would do something wrong and I would get really upset about it whereas now it's a case of, ‘whoops’.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay are there any other students on placement with you?

Subject:	No I’m the only one.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would have been helpful to have other students on placement on the same site as you?

Subject:	Erm, I think possibly erm mainly because then you could compare experiences and see what’s going on. But on the other hand and I it sort of comes back down to the same thing, if I’d had sort of you know a [Company] engineer or someone assigned to me, slightly more senior that I could have gone to and spoken to about my problems I don't think it would have made necessarily all that much difference. But I think it could be good if you just like if you’ve had a bad day to have gone and spoken to someone but everyone you know – I mean I've done some fairly horrific things so far. I've managed to put the back of a machine right through a water main but when you think, and you go ‘oh god’, but then everybody on the site can come out with you know one better story, ‘well actually I've done this so’. You don't necessarily have to be a student you just, in fact experience in that case is better because they can all go ‘well I've done this and I've done that and I've done the other’. You feel so much better knowing that I'm not the only one that makes horrendous mistakes.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay do you feel that you're treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

Subject:	Erm by the management yes. (Yeah) By some of the people on site no they really do have a, ‘oh she’s a student and she doesn’t know anything’, attitude. (Yeah) But I tend to ignore them anyway.

Interviewer:	OK do you is most of your work team work?

Subject:	Erm sort of I mean in that er in the beginning a lot of it was quite sort of you know just like the engineer doing the work. But now it's quite sort of directly related to like the labour so it was like last night we were putting in like a drainage run and I was controlling the levels of the concrete they were pouring. So as they're pouring it I'm checking the levels it's like ‘oh no that’s too high that’s too low, a bit more here, a bit less there’ so now and that’s just one example but there's a lot of stuff that goes on like that and we’re there controlling it, (yeah) and they're working.

Interviewer:	How do you feel that doing team work at work compares to doing team work at uni?

Subject:	Oh I think at work it's a bit more sort of you know, while yeah everyone is sort of messing round you know sort of being friendly and stuff and you know that half the time you're only being friendly with them because you're at work. (Yeah) And it's a bit more critical and I feel at work you have to pull your weight whereas at uni sometimes you get people you know you're in a group and they're just in there along for the ride. Whereas at work generally if you're not pulling your weight, especially like in the construction industry, if you're not pulling your weight you just get sacked. (Yeah) Because there's been a few people like that who just wouldn’t seem to do any work and didn’t join in and they're just not there the next day.

Interviewer:	Okay in that way then do you think that it's easier or harder doing team work in the workplace?

Subject:	Erm, I well I have never been one of the people to just let, you know sit back and have a ride along while everyone else has the work finished so erm but I think it depends, it's quite hard to explain it. I think in some ways it's easier at uni because you can all just sort of pile in together and you all sort help each other out. Because while we’re doing team work at work, at the end of the day, with a lot of the stuff I am you know it's still sort of my call. I decide whether it's right or wrong. (Yeah) There's still quite a lot of responsibility.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay do you think that doing team work at uni does help and prepare you for doing group work at work then?

Subject:	Yes it does. I think it does because obviously you don't get on with everybody, you're never going to, and I think working with people at uni erm especially if you don't get on with them particularly well I think that has helped me to, you know, it doesn’t matter whether I like somebody or not I can work with them you know and I've realised it doesn’t matter whether you like someone or not, you just learn to work with them and I think that’s helped a lot. Because I mean there's people like that at work you know if you sort of met them out of work you sort of wouldn’t know them, but we work and we can get on fine and have laugh and everything.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay have you been given any mentor at all within the company?

Subject:	Erm not really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that would have been a good idea?

Subject:	I think so yes like I said everything like that that’s happened has been through my instigation. (Yeah) It would have been nice to have someone to say, right I'm in charge, I'm in charge of your welfare. You know because when things go wrong everyone is like oh but of course I'm interested. Of course I care you must talk to me, you must talk to me but nobody ever sort of said that right back at the start. When I walked in nobody ever said if you have any problems you come to me. So I think yeah some sort of guide.

Interviewer:	Ok is there anyone that you would say you have treated as a mentor or anyone in particular that you tend to go to for advice and things?

Subject:	Yeah well there's a person that’s my external tutor, he’s the agent which is the person in charge of the section I'm working on. There's 3 main sections on the job and there's an agent in charge of each one and then there's the Project Manager and he’s in charge of them and I think I have tended to have gone to him the most with my problems. Mainly because he has the most day to day contact but in that respect sometimes because they're all men and in that respect sometimes it would be nice to have someone female. Just when someone has said something to me and I'm a bit upset and I don't know, sometimes it feels like talking to a woman would be sometimes easier.

Interviewer:	Yeah because they would understand more from your perspective?

Subject:	Yeah you know what’s it like when you're being a bit girlie and you're having a little cry or something and it's not and I find sometimes when I get fed up with the men they tend to take it seriously and I'm like, ‘no it's not serious I'm just having a little moment’ (Yeah) And I think sometimes yeah because you can just say to them all, ‘I'm having a little moment’ and they sort of go, ‘right I know where you're coming from’, rather than it being very serious.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model at all then?

Subject:	Erm I haven’t really seen anyone within the company except for those few of them on my site. (Yeah) Erm, I think well the way people deal with their crises and things going wrong. I mean most of the people on there I sort of look at them and think I wish I could deal with it as calmly as that. And I wish when things are wrong I could just sort of go, ‘oh never mind’ and carry on and solve it but again I think that’s all part of the experience of growing up.

Interviewer:	Yes definitely. okay has anyone from university - lecturers or anything been to visit you on placement?

Subject:	Yes, yes I've had a few visits.

Interviewer:	And did they explain like the purpose of the visit and stuff like that?

Subject:	Yes they did yes they had like little sheets to fill out as well (OK) about the visit.

Interviewer:	Was it someone that you knew the person that came to visit you?

Subject:	Er the first time it wasn’t, I had never even to be honest never actually heard of him till he rang me up. (OK) But he decided afterwards because he wasn’t actually a civil engineering lecturer. (Right) He was a transport lecturer because there were 2 other people working at the airport they thought they would combine them all. (Right okay) But he decided that he was sort of way out of his depth coming to see me. You know I was telling him what I had been doing and he didn’t understand. (Yeah) So he couldn’t sort of you know he didn’t know whether it was good, bad. So then I had another lecturer who I did know, (Yeah) who was a civils lecturer come and see me.

Interviewer:	OK so was that much better?

Subject:	I thought so yes because well for starters I knew him and it was easy to sort of I could talk to him rather than like, ‘oh this is the first time I've ever met you’ and you know I felt a lot more relaxed and less formal. Plus they knew what I was talking about which made a big difference you know when he said, ‘oh so what have you been doing’? I started talking he and I you know he was actually listening rather than just writing it all down.

Interviewer:	Yeah okay did they speak to your manager as well or your agent?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	About the work that you’ve been doing?

Subject:	Yes they did a bit.

Interviewer:	Ok would you or have you discussed either with the placement tutors any sort of problems that you’ve been having like?

Subject:	Yes I did that was actually why I ended up, well I was going to be getting a second visit anyway but I got one much quicker because I was having erm massive problems with this guy. He was erm well very sexist and had big problems with me being a student and sort of slagged me off to every single person on the site. Like I said some of which I knew about so and I could only guess at what he said about me when I wasn’t there. (Yeah) And erm and I got quite upset and down about this so I rang up and he was on the phone to another person literally the next day and he had come to see me within a week.

Interviewer:	That’s good.

Subject:	So I thought it was very good considering he was coming from [university] and you know he had been to see me within a week of me making the first phone call. And I was on the phone to him sort of about 2 or 3 times during that week and there he was like calling me back, you know if they weren’t in and I left a message they would sort of phone me back and they were just phoning me up, so.

Interviewer:	Did you find did they offer you any helpful advice then?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah and what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject

(Yeah) Because I just feel that if it had all been organised properly I’d have been sort of much happier and much more able just to relax and learn.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes okay how would you say that the placement has met your expectations then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yes I've got a very well I feel I've got a very sort of varied experience. Well I will have by the time I've finished in what I've been doing. I've you know I've been involved in sort of all different areas of the construction because I've been there right from the very start. I've been involved in all of the different things like the sort of black top laying and the drainage and constructing sort of electricity cable runs and things like that. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes okay is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm not sure I mean I think I sort of came out, you know I sort expect that I’d know sort of a bit of a, to be able to just come out and do everything. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what do you think are the main benefits of doing a placement are then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think erm God like I said I'm not sure that I want to go into civil engineering erm I've got the rest of this year to think plus the next 2 years at university to think about it. Plus there's lots of the practical aspects that you can apply to all the theory now. Like the things I've learnt and well I can think about the work and think, ‘oh yeah well when he says that he actually means this because now I know what he’s talking about’. (Yeah) And hopefully when we go back and do more work I’ll be able to do it the other way around. (Yeah) And sort of theoretical I’ll then be able to think of the practical and think, ‘ah yeah well I remember doing this’. So you know and sort I will be able to sort of visualise the practical side.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't think so really I could only think it would be a drawback if you went into it and decided that you absolutely hated it but on the other hand again that would still be a good thing because you would have only sort of wasted a year as opposed to…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Your whole career.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Erm no I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do you think that you have changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so I think I've grown up a bit, realised that things go wrong but even if I do it wrong it's not me personally even though I may have done it wrong it's not you know, if I get shouted at they're not, they're not shouting at me personally you know I get shouted at because I did it wrong but then that’s it, end of story. (Yeah) So yeah I think I've grown up and learnt to or learning I should say not to take things quite so personally. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay are there any other students on placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I’m the only one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would have been helpful to have other students on placement on the same site as you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think possibly erm mainly because then you could compare experiences and see what’s going on. But on the other hand and I it sort of comes back down to the same thing, if I’d had sort of you know a [Company] engineer or someone assigned to me, slightly more senior that I could have gone to and spoken to about my problems I don't think it would have made necessarily all that much difference. But I think it could be good if you just like if you’ve had a bad day to have gone and spoken to someone but everyone you know – I mean I've done some fairly horrific things so far. I've managed to put the back of a machine right through a water main but when you think, and you go ‘oh god’, but then everybody on the site can come out with you know one better story, ‘well actually I've done this so’. You don't necessarily have to be a student you just, in fact experience in that case is better because they can all go ‘well I've done this and I've done that and I've done the other’. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay do you feel that you're treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm by the management yes. (Yeah) By some of the people on site no they really do have a, ‘oh she’s a student and she doesn’t know anything’, attitude. (Yeah) But I tend to ignore them anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you is most of your work team work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm sort of I mean in that er in the beginning a lot of it was quite sort of you know just like the engineer doing the work. So as they're pouring it I'm checking the levels it's like ‘oh no that’s too high that’s too low, a bit more here, a bit less there’ so now and that’s just one example but there's a lot of stuff that goes on like that and we’re there controlling it, (yeah) and they're working.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel that doing team work at work compares to doing team work at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I think at work it's a bit more sort of you know, while yeah everyone is sort of messing round you know sort of being friendly and stuff and you know that half the time you're only being friendly with them because you're at work. (Yeah) And it's a bit more critical and I feel at work you have to pull your weight whereas at uni sometimes you get people you know you're in a group and they're just in there along for the ride. Whereas at work generally if you're not pulling your weight, especially like in the construction industry, if you're not pulling your weight you just get sacked. (Yeah) Because there's been a few people like that who just wouldn’t seem to do any work and didn’t join in and they're just not there the next day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay in that way then do you think that it's easier or harder doing team work in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I well I have never been one of the people to just let, you know sit back and have a ride along while everyone else has the work finished so erm but I think it depends, it's quite hard to explain it. I think in some ways it's easier at uni because you can all just sort of pile in together and you all sort help each other out. Because while we’re doing team work at work, at the end of the day, with a lot of the stuff I am you know it's still sort of my call. I decide whether it's right or wrong. (Yeah) There's still quite a lot of responsibility.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay do you think that doing team work at uni does help and prepare you for doing group work at work then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it does. I think it does because obviously you don't get on with everybody, you're never going to, and I think working with people at uni erm especially if you don't get on with them particularly well I think that has helped me to, you know, it doesn’t matter whether I like somebody or not I can work with them you know and I've realised it doesn’t matter whether you like someone or not, you just learn to work with them and I think that’s helped a lot. Because I mean there's people like that at work you know if you sort of met them out of work you sort of wouldn’t know them, but we work and we can get on fine and have laugh and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay have you been given any mentor at all within the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that would have been a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yes like I said everything like that that’s happened has been through my instigation. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok is there anyone that you would say you have treated as a mentor or anyone in particular that you tend to go to for advice and things?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah because they would understand more from your perspective?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah you know what’s it like when you're being a bit girlie and you're having a little cry or something and it's not and I find sometimes when I get fed up with the men they tend to take it seriously and I'm like, ‘no it's not serious I'm just having a little moment’ (Yeah) And I think sometimes yeah because you can just say to them all, ‘I'm having a little moment’ and they sort of go, ‘right I know where you're coming from’, rather than it being very serious.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model at all then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I haven’t really seen anyone within the company except for those few of them on my site. (Yeah) Erm, I think well the way people deal with their crises and things going wrong. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes definitely. okay has anyone from university - lecturers or anything been to visit you on placement?

turns.text: Yes, yes I've had a few visits.

turns.text: And did they explain like the purpose of the visit and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes they did yes they had like little sheets to fill out as well (OK) about the visit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it someone that you knew the person that came to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK so was that much better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I thought so yes because well for starters I knew him and it was easy to sort of I could talk to him rather than like, ‘oh this is the first time I've ever met you’ and you know I felt a lot more relaxed and less formal. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay did they speak to your manager as well or your agent?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: About the work that you’ve been doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes they did a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok would you or have you discussed either with the placement tutors any sort of problems that you’ve been having like?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So I thought it was very good considering he was coming from [university] and you know he had been to see me within a week of me making the first phone call. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you find did they offer you any helpful advice then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I thought they did yeah I mean a lot of it was just basic you know like oh don't you know don't get upset about this and general advice but I was telling them my problems and I felt that they were actually interested. (Yeah) You know they were interested and they wanted to solve them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah do you think it was easier to talk to someone at university about the problems than it was to talk to someone in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I did I'm not quite sure really why I think because at work I was very conscious you know of wanting to be sort of professional and thinking about the future and not wanting to be the one that has got all of these, these sorts of problems you know and again I think I don't know really why I think I just felt that uni was easier to approach.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay do you know whether either the work place or at university have a complaints procedure to follow if you did have any serious problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, as far as I'm aware the first at work the first step is to go to a member of senior management with your complaint and then they deal with it from there whether they need to tell it to somebody else or talk to the people potentially involved. turns.text: Okay do you feel that there are appropriate facilities for women on site?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er yes. There's only actually 3 so, there’s literally 3 women on site so...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok so have you got women’s toilets?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah we've got well we've just got the one but erm it's like I said there's only 3 women so one toilet it's adequate and there's all the sort of necessary bins and what nots?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And yeah do you have to wear safety clothing and stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And does that all fit?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes that was good then.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But that was that actually generally applies to everyone as well. (Yeah) To an extent if you need something they can order it in your size. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay you’ve said a couple of things already but can you think of any occasions where you feel like your gender has determined reactions that you’ve got from people or the put come of particular events?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm sometimes well a lot of the time it works to my advantage I think when I've gone down and said to somebody, ‘oh can you come and do this for me in a bit’? And they're like, ‘of course I can’ then sort of 5 minutes later they (inaudible) or I go to someone ‘can you help me with this’ or ‘can you do that’ or really little things like someone has parked their van over in the way of where we need to work. I've found that if I've go over and ask, a lot of the time I’ll get, generally speaking they’ll move anyway, but sometimes they're a bit stubborn and if I go and ask a lot of the time I’ll get a much faster response. So it does work to my advantage a lot of the time. You’ll get obviously people that do, I’ve said already, people that do have issues with it, and a lot of it mostly is you know just bits of friendly banter. Most of it sadly from men that are about 50 so you have to like, you have you take it. I mean I was sort of saying to one person you know you it's like you look at these guys and you say if they thought that you know you thought they were being serious I think they would drop down on the spot. Because it's only ever joking and sort of more affectionate I think in a way like they sort of looking out for you in a way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of what any sort of examples of any types of jokes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh like, oh like if I'm cold you know I’ll be sort of stood there and cold and shivering and they’ll say, ‘oh would you like me to warm you up’? ‘Do you want to get in my coat’ and ‘I’ll warm you up’ and things like that? Well when you're stood there and they're like grabbing your hands and they're like ‘oh I’ll keep your hands warm for you’ and things like that and I’ll say, ‘oh lovely that’s so nice of you’. Erm yes that sort of the main types of jokes really ones they sort of drop your foot in it and like wandering over and saying to someone, ‘oh well, did you want me’, and they’re like ‘well…’ and it's just like ‘no’. Do you know what I mean, it’s that sort of. I mean I’ve found it all to be very jokey and I don't think anybody has said anything sort of dodgy or sexually related sort of stuff that I've taken offence to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, so you were saying earlier that you don't know if you want to stay in civil engineering. Do you think did you felt like that before you started the placement or do you think it is a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think it's more a result of the placement erm and at the moment I think it's just I've been sort of thinking about things like working outside when it's cold and raining and I'm not sure how long I want to do that for. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah so maybe go into the consultancy?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. Well it's an option before I just went oh I'm never doing civil engineering I would certainly explore that first. What my current plan of action as it were is sort of finish this year go back to uni, go through uni, see how it goes and then I’ll probably go out and go to different sites. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It might be different.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah you know people might actually want to be there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that your placement will experience will help you when you graduate even if you go into a different area?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so because like I said I've learnt to deal with people and I've learnt to accept that not everyone is going to like me and I'm not going to like everyone. So I think that’d help in any industry sort of perfecting the art of just getting on with people at work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay do you think that the experience will help you cope when you start work after graduation sort of in terms of getting on in a male environment and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so because erm it's every time you know it's always just getting used to it and you just don't notice it almost. So I think yeah working like that and sort of things like you know having to go to the toilet and you know having to go back to the toilet rather than pop behind the nearest van and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah okay would you work for [Company] when you graduate if they offered you a place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think I would have to speak to them first I think I would speak to them first and explain why I wasn’t particularly happy with my placement. You know or the fact that I'm a student and I am learning and they sort of wanted another body to do the work. I think I would speak to them about it first but if they could you know sort of addressed those conditions. Address those sort of issues then yes I would.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay would you recommend someone else to do a placement with [Company]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, at the moment no because the financial state of the company’s so up in the air. There's major reorganisations going on and there's none of the you know we've got Directors and they don't know if they're going to be out of a job next week at the moment so.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think it's hard, very erm now what’s the word you need to be very dedicated I think. Erm I think in a way quite exciting because again it's all about you know like I started off back in October and there was a field and now it's got you know most of a taxi way running through it and I find that very exciting to think oh well I did that. Erm, I can't think of any more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s okay what would you say are the main advantages and disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think disadvantages like I said you get people that just, just have issues with you for no reason other than the fact that you are a girl and they think you should be at home cooking and cleaning. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they remember you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So yeah and so like if they're being directed, oh I’ll go and find Hannah she is up here. And life I said, the sort of obvious like you get you know people are more, then again especially the slightly older men, you know I'm probably the same age as their daughters and stuff like that, they’ll help you out a little bit more, do things for you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that more women should be encouraged into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so because I think there's no reason why women can't do like I said okay there are some of the heavy lifting things that you can't do but there's always enough people around. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah do you think that it will the situation will improve for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, I think gradually like I mean a few years ago you know you would not have any sort of women in it and I think gradually as you know more and more girls go through uni and stuff it will gradually become one of those things that everybody does. turns.speaker: Interviewer
